title: Keeping the Heat Moving: How a Data Centre Stays Cool

narration: Say this is your data hall.
Rows of servers, a steady hum.
beats.visual_intent: A blueprint plan of one data hall: rows of racks drawn in line, still and calm, seen from above at an angle.

grounding.claim: an example data hall

narration: Every server here turns its power into heat.
Almost all of it, all the time.
beats.visual_intent: The same plan; heat marks rise from every rack at once, power lines feeding in, so the still hall is suddenly visibly busy.

grounding.claim: servers turn almost all the power they draw into heat, continuously

narration: So where does that heat go?
And what if it stopped going?
beats.visual_intent: The heat marks gather above the hall with nowhere to go; the question hangs over the open drawing.

grounding.claim: a hypothetical question about lost cooling

narration: Let's follow it out, link by link.
beats.visual_intent: A faint chain of four links drawn across the building section, from rack to roof, each link only outlined for now.

grounding.claim: heat travels outward through a chain of parts to the outdoors

narration: Think of a fridge.
It doesn't make cold.
It moves heat out of the box.
beats.visual_intent: A fridge in section: heat arrows travel from inside the box, through the back coil, out into the room around it.
beats.misconception: cooling makes cold and destroys heat

grounding.claim: cooling moves heat rather than making cold

narration: A data hall does the same, at building scale.
The heat is carried outside.
beats.visual_intent: Pull back from the fridge to the whole building section; one long heat path runs from the hall up and out through the roof.

grounding.claim: heat is moved and ends up outdoors

narration: First link: the air.
Racks stand in rows,
fronts facing fronts, backs facing backs.
beats.visual_intent: Plan view of the hall: rack rows turn to show fronts facing fronts and backs facing backs, the aisles between them marked.

grounding.claim: racks face front to front and back to back across aisles

narration: Here, cool air rises through the floor
into the aisle the fronts share:
the cold aisle.
beats.visual_intent: Section through the hall: cool air arrows travel under the raised floor and rise through perforated tiles into the front aisle, which is then labelled.

grounding.claim: cold air is often delivered through a raised floor
the cold aisle is the one the fronts face

narration: Servers pull it in at the front
and blow it out warm at the back:
the hot aisle.
beats.visual_intent: The same section: cool arrows enter the rack fronts, change colour through the servers, and leave the backs warm into the next aisle.

grounding.claim: servers draw air in the front and exhaust it warm out the back
the backs face the hot aisle

narration: The warm air returns to tall cabinets at the hall's edge,
called computer room air handlers.
beats.visual_intent: Warm arrows travel along the ceiling to tall cabinets at the hall's edge; one cabinet is outlined and labelled as it is named.

grounding.claim: a CRAH takes in hot return air

narration: A coil of chilled water takes the heat,
and the air goes back out cool.
beats.visual_intent: Cutaway of the CRAH: warm air passes over a coil of water pipes, the heat moves into the coil, and cool air leaves under the floor.

grounding.claim: the CRAH cools air across a chilled water coil and blows cold air back
the water absorbs heat at the coil

narration: Keep the aisles apart.
Hot air leaking back makes hot spots
and wastes cooling.
Closing one aisle off is called containment.
beats.visual_intent: Warm arrows curl over the rack tops into the cold aisle and the upper servers glow; then doors and roof panels close over the aisle and the flows separate cleanly.
beats.misconception: more cold air anywhere is enough

grounding.claim: mixing hot exhaust into supply air creates hot spots and wastes cooling
containment closes off an aisle to keep hot and cold air apart

narration: ASHRAE recommends inlet air
between 18 and 27 degrees Celsius.
beats.visual_intent: A thermometer at one server's front intake with the recommended band marked between 18 and 27.

grounding.claim: ASHRAE recommended server inlet range 18 to 27 degrees Celsius

narration: Second link: the water.
Leaving the coil, it is warmer now.
beats.visual_intent: From the CRAH coil, a pipe leaves the hall; the water in it is drawn warmer as it heads away.

grounding.claim: the water leaves the coil warmer after absorbing heat

narration: Pumps push it round a closed loop
to the plant room and back.
beats.visual_intent: The building section shows the full pipe loop; a pump's impeller turns and the water visibly circulates round the loop.

grounding.claim: pumps keep the water circulating around the loop

narration: There, the chiller pulls the heat out,
like your fridge,
and sends the water back cold.
beats.visual_intent: Cutaway of the chiller: warm water enters, heat is drawn out into its refrigerant circuit, cold water leaves back toward the hall.

grounding.claim: a chiller removes heat from returning water with a refrigeration cycle and returns it cold

narration: Third link: outside.
A cooling tower or dry cooler
releases the heat into the air.
beats.visual_intent: The heat path climbs from the chiller to a unit on the roof; heat lifts off it into the open sky.

grounding.claim: outdoor equipment such as a cooling tower or dry cooler releases the heat to the outdoor air

narration: Server, air, air handler, water, pump, chiller, outdoors.
Each link hands the heat on.
beats.visual_intent: The whole building section with the chain of links lit one after another as each is named, heat passing along it.

recall.prompt: Name the links in order, from the server to the outdoor air.

grounding.claim: servers exhaust heat into air
the CRAH passes heat to water
pumps move the water
the chiller takes heat from the water
outdoor equipment releases it

narration: Now, say one air handler fails.
This hall is N plus one:
enough units for the load, plus one spare.
beats.visual_intent: In the hall plan one CRAH's fan stops and it turns to a failed state; the row is counted, the units carrying the load bracketed as N and one more marked as the spare.
beats.delivery: even, reassuring; slow down on N plus one

grounding.claim: a hypothetical air handler failure
N+1 means the units needed plus one spare

narration: In a well designed system,
the spare starts by itself,
and the hall keeps its capacity.
beats.visual_intent: Before and after: the spare unit's fan spins up and its air arrows fill the gap left by the failed one, flows back to normal.

grounding.claim: a standby unit starts automatically through the control system
one unit can fail without losing capacity

narration: Sensors raise an alarm for repair,
and cold water in the pipes buys time.
That is ride-through.
beats.visual_intent: A sensor flags the failed unit on a monitoring panel; the pipe loop and a buffer tank stay full of cold water, a reserve draining slowly while the spare takes over.

grounding.claim: sensors and monitoring raise alarms so operators can respond
chilled water in the pipes helps the hall ride through a changeover

narration: Lose cooling for good, and the room warms.
Servers slow down or shut off.
Spares keep it from coming to that.
beats.visual_intent: A temperature readout climbs with no number given and servers dim to a throttled state, then the picture returns to the spare running.

grounding.claim: without restored cooling, temperature rises and servers may throttle or shut down

narration: Your turn.
Say one pump stops.
What happens next?
beats.visual_intent: The pipe loop with one pump marked stopped; the question held on screen, nothing else moving.

recall.prompt: One pump in an N+1 loop stops. What happens next?
recall.answer: the standby pump starts; the alarm calls an operator; the water in the loop covers the changeover

grounding.claim: a hypothetical pump failure

narration: The standby pump starts.
The alarm calls an operator.
Water in the loop covers the gap.
beats.visual_intent: The answer plays out on the loop: the standby pump spins up, the alarm points to the stopped one, water keeps circulating.

grounding.claim: a standby pump starts automatically
the alarm prompts operators to respond
water in the loop helps ride through the changeover

narration: Back in the quiet hall,
you can see the heat moving out,
with spares standing by.
beats.visual_intent: The opening hall plan again, now with every flow drawn running: air through the aisles, water round the loop, heat off the roof, spares outlined.

grounding.claim: heat is carried outdoors through the chain
spare units stand by

narration: Next cooling alarm you hear of, ask:
which link failed,
and did its spare take over?
beats.visual_intent: The two questions sit beside the finished building drawing, the chain still running behind them.

grounding.claim: standby units take over when one fails
